items.section_title: 17.4 · Objective a — Normal structures on computed tomography and the angiogram
items.html: Why the trachea and bronchi are dark on computed tomography. Air and gas are low attenuation, so the air-filled trachea and bronchi show dark on computed tomography.

src.question: A 44-year-old's lung-window computed tomography shows the trachea and main bronchi as dark circles. Why are they dark?
src.explanation: Air and gas are low attenuation, so the air-filled trachea and bronchi show dark on computed tomography.

items.section_title: 20.2 · Objective a — The four lung volumes and the four lung capacities
items.html: Total lung capacity is the sum of all four volumes. Total lung capacity, the maximum volume the lungs can hold, is the sum of all four volumes: tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 13 and 23

src.question: A 60-year-old woman's report lists the maximum volume of air her lungs can hold. Which volumes add up to it?
src.key: All four volumes, residual volume included
src.explanation: Correct. Total lung capacity, the maximum volume the lungs can hold, is the sum of all four volumes: tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual.

items.section_title: 20.6 · Objective d — Interpreting a report: the stepwise read and three cases
items.html: A low total lung capacity is restriction. A low total lung capacity is restriction; with a normal ratio there is no obstruction alongside it.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 43 and 32

src.question: A 57-year-old woman's total lung capacity is 62% of predicted (normal 80% to 120%), with an FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio of 88% (normal above 80%). What is the basic interpretation?
src.explanation: Correct. A low total lung capacity is restriction, and her ratio is normal, so there is no obstruction alongside it.

items.section_title: 20.3 · Objective a — Spirometry: how it is done and the forced values
items.html: The spirometry breath out. After a maximal breath in, the patient exhales forcefully, as fast as possible, and keeps going for at least 6 seconds.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 24, 29 and 21

src.question: A 45-year-old man is coached through spirometry. After he breathes in as deeply as he can, what is he asked to do?
src.key: Blow out as hard and fast as he can for 6 seconds or more
src.explanation: Correct. After a maximal breath in, the patient exhales forcefully, as fast as possible, and keeps going for at least 6 seconds.

items.section_title: 20.7 · Objective e — The role of pulmonary function testing in diagnosis and monitoring
items.html: Lung volumes diagnose restriction. Lung volumes are the standard test responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease; spirometry diagnoses obstruction and the diffusing capacity pulmonary vascular disease.
cites: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 18 and 43

src.question: A 63-year-old man's spirometry suggests restriction. Which standard test is responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease?
src.explanation: Correct. Lung volumes are the standard test responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease; spirometry diagnoses obstruction and the diffusing capacity pulmonary vascular disease.
